slides.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
slides.body:
Definition
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a simple, connectionless transport layer protocol that sends data between applications with minimal overhead, but does not guarantee delivery, ordering, or reliability

slides.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
slides.body:
Key Characteristics of UDP
Connectionless:No setup before sending
Unreliable:No delivery guarantee, no acknowledgments
No Ordering:Datagrams may arrive out of order
No Flow or Congestion Control:Sender does not adjust speed

slides.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
slides.body:
Key Characteristics of UDP
Stateless:Each datagram is independent
Fast & Lightweight:Minimal overhead
Low Latency:No Retransmission delays

slides.title: UDP Datagram
slides.body:
Structure and Size Limitations
For data units at the Transport Layer, different protocols use different names:
In UDP, the data unit is called a Datagram (or User Datagram)

slides.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
slides.body:
What does it actually do?
Takes data from the application
Adds a small header (source port, destination port, length, checksum)
Hands it to the Network Layer for delivery
UDP does the bare minimum:
That is it. No handshakes, no retransmissions, no ordering

slides.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy: UDP is like shouting a message across a crowded room. You shout it once and hope the other person hears it. You do not wait for them to confirm. You do not repeat it if they missed it. You do not even check if they are still in the room. It is fast, but there is no guarantee.

slides.title: UDP Header
slides.body:
Simple and Small
Total Header Size: 8 bytes only. Compare this with TCP which has a minimum header of 20 bytes (and can go up to 60 bytes). This tiny header is one reason why UDP is so fast — less overhead per packet

slides.title: UDP Header
slides.body:
Important Notes
Length Field: Specifies total datagram size (header + data). Minimum value = 8 bytes (header size)
Checksum: Detects corruption. If corrupted, the datagram is discarded (no retransmission)

Structure and Size Limitations
Key Point
UDP does not split or reassemble data. It sends application data as a single datagram. If the datagram is too large, IP(Network Layer) handles fragmentation, not UDP

slides.title: TCP Segment — The Data Unit of TCP
slides.body:
Maximum Segment Size (MSS)
MSS defines the maximum amount of data (not including the header) that a TCP segment can carry
MSS is negotiated during the TCP connection setup (3-way handshake)
Typical MSS value: 1460 bytes (Ethernet MTU 1500 - 20 bytes IP header - 20 bytes TCP header = 1460 bytes)

slides.title: TCP Segment — The Data Unit of TCP
slides.body:
Analogy: Imagine you need to send a 500-page book to a friend. UDP would try to stuff the entire book into one envelope. TCP would divide the book into chapters, number each chapter (sequence number), put each in a separate envelope, and the friend would reassemble the book in order at the other end. If chapter 5 gets lost, TCP makes sure it gets resent.

slides.title: TCP vs UDP — Side by Side
slides.body:
A Detailed Comparison
Both TCP and UDP use port numbers for multiplexing and demultiplexing
Both use checksums for error detection, but TCP retransmits lost data, while UDP simply discards it
TCP adds overhead for reliability and data integrity

slides.title: Choosing Between TCP and UDP
slides.body:
Applications that use BOTH
Application
DNS
How?
Uses UDP for regular queries (fast). Uses TCP for zone transfers and large responses (>512 bytes)
Streaming (Netflix, YouTube)
Uses TCP (via HTTPS) for video delivery; may use UDP-based protocols for lower latency

slides.title: Why Not Just Always Use TCP?
slides.body:
Understanding TCP’s Trade-offs
This is a common question:
"If TCP guarantees delivery, why would anyone use UDP?"

slides.title: Why Not Just Always Use TCP?
slides.body:
Understanding TCP’s Trade-offs
Connection Delay: Requires a 3-way handshake → adds extra latency (at least 1 RTT)
No Broadcast/Multicast: Supports only one-to-one communication
If TCP guarantees delivery, why use UDP?
The Cost of TCP Reliability

slides.title: Why Not Just Always Use TCP?
slides.body:
Understanding TCP’s Trade-offs
Congestion Control: Slows down transmission during congestion → not ideal for real-time apps
Head-of-Line Blocking: One lost packet delays all following packets → causes freezes in real-time apps
Higher Overhead: 20-byte header (vs 8 bytes in UDP) → inefficient for small messages
If TCP guarantees delivery, why use UDP?
The Cost of TCP Reliability

slides.title: Why Not Just Always Use TCP?
slides.body:
Understanding TCP’s Trade-offs
Key Observations
TCP’s reliability comes at a cost — latency, overhead, and rigidity. For applications where speed and real-time performance matter more than perfection, UDP is the better choice
